guide.title: Celio, Rome: the Colosseum, the Caelian hill and the road to the Porta Latina
guide.intro: Celio is the nineteenth of Rome's rioni by toponymic code, and it is two pieces of ground rather than one. The northern piece is the Caelian hill, which Roma Capitale records was anciently called Mons Querquetulanus because it was covered in oaks. The Colosseum stands on its western edge, and so do a free archaeological park with two museums in it, a group of early basilicas, and the walled Mattei garden that is now the public park of Villa Celimontana. The southern piece is a long tongue of ground running inside the Aurelian Walls down via di Porta San Sebastiano, carrying the tomb of the Scipios, a painted columbarium, two churches at the Porta Latina and the city nursery that grows the azaleas for the Spanish Steps. Almost every edge of the rione is a street shared with a neighbour, which is why several things a visitor would reasonably file under Celio are not written on this page.

sections.heading: What is in Celio, and what is not
sections.body:
it.wikipedia's article on the rione reproduces Celio's delimitation, and reading it is the fastest way to understand why this page carries what it carries. The line with Monti runs along piazza del Colosseo, via di San Giovanni in Laterano, via Santo Stefano Rotondo and via della Navicella to piazza di Porta Metronia. The south-east side is the Aurelian Walls themselves, from Porta Metronia to Porta San Sebastiano, with the quartiere of Appio-Latino beyond them. The line with San Saba runs along via di Porta San Sebastiano, piazzale Numa Pompilio, a short stretch of viale delle Terme di Caracalla, via di Valle delle Camene and piazza di Porta Capena. To the west are Ripa, at piazza di Porta Capena, and Campitelli, along via di San Gregorio and piazza del Colosseo. A street named as a boundary tells you where a line runs; it does not tell you what stands on either side of it.

The Colosseum is in Celio and is written here. Two churches whose names point at the Caelian are not: the basilica of Santo Stefano Rotondo al Celio carries the hill in its title, but via di Santo Stefano Rotondo is the line with Monti, and both Santo Stefano Rotondo and San Clemente are written under Monti in this series, along with San Giovanni in Laterano and the park of Colle Oppio.

Four more things a visitor may expect here are deliberately absent. Roma Capitale addresses the Arch of Constantine to via di San Gregorio, which the delimitation names as the line with Campitelli, and neither the arch nor the ruins of the Meta Sudans are written on this page. it.wikipedia's article on the rione states that the start of the Appia Antica at Porta San Sebastiano is shared to the east between rione Celio and rione San Saba, so neither the gate nor the Museo delle Mura inside it is written here; note in any case that the museum's own site carries a notice that the museum is not accessible. The Porta Latina stands on the same wall line and is likewise not written here, though the basilica and the oratory that take their names from it are. And the Terme di Caracalla, whose viale clips the rione's southern boundary, stand in San Saba.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
For the northern lobe, the Parco archeologico del Colosseo gives access to piazza del Colosseo as Metro line B, station Colosseo; buses 51, 75, 81, 85, 87 and 118; and tram 3. Everything on the Caelian shoulder is reached from that square on foot, and the rest of this section is addresses rather than distances.

The Parco archeologico del Celio has three entrances, which the Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives as Viale del Parco del Celio 20, Viale del Parco del Celio 22 and Clivo di Scauro 4; the Museo della Forma Urbis and the Casina del Salvi are both at Viale del Parco del Celio 20. The basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo is at Piazza dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo 13, and the Case Romane del Celio are entered from the Clivo di Scauro, which Roma Capitale describes as an ancient Roman road and the principal axis of the Caelian, keeping part of its original course. San Gregorio al Celio is at Piazza di San Gregorio 1, with the park behind it entered from Salita di San Gregorio 3. Villa Celimontana has entrances on via della Navicella and on piazza dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo, and Santa Maria in Domnica faces the fountain of the Navicella at Via della Navicella 10. The complex of the Santi Quattro Coronati is at Via dei Santi Quattro 20.

The southern lobe is a walk of its own and no source states a bus route or a station for it, so none is given here. Steer by via di Porta San Sebastiano and via di Porta Latina. The Sepolcro degli Scipioni is at Via di Porta San Sebastiano 9. The Parco degli Scipioni has two entrances, Via di Porta Latina 10 and one on via di Porta San Sebastiano that the Sovrintendenza Capitolina records as currently closed; the Colombario di Pomponio Hylas is inside it, addressed by Roma Capitale to Via di Porta Latina 10. San Giovanni a Porta Latina is at Via di Porta Latina 17 and the oratory of San Giovanni in Oleo at no. 77. Piazzale Numa Pompilio carries San Sisto Vecchio at no. 8 and the Parco Egerio, and the Semenzaio di San Sisto is on Via Druso at no. 2.

sections.heading: Tickets, hours and closures
sections.body:
No current opening hours for the Colosseum are given here. Times and last admission change with the season; the Parco archeologico del Colosseo publishes them at colosseo.it, and tickets are sold at ticketing.colosseo.it. The Museo del Colosseo is on the second level of the amphitheatre and is reached on the same visit.

Around it, a good deal is free. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the Parco archeologico del Celio as free to enter, open 7.00 to 17.30 in winter and 7.00 to 20.00 in summer, closed on 25 December and 1 May, and states that the archaeological area and the museum are accessible to all. In the same park, the Museo della Forma Urbis opens Tuesday to Sunday, 10.00 to 16.00 in winter with last entry at 15.00 and 10.00 to 19.00 in summer with last entry at 18.00, closed Mondays, 25 December and 1 May; the Casina del Salvi serves as a caffetteria and study room daily, 9.00 to 16.30 in winter and 9.00 to 19.00 in summer.

For the churches, Roma Capitale publishes the hours of Santi Giovanni e Paolo as 08.30 to 12.45 and 14.00 to 17.00, with the note that some times may vary during the wedding season, and gives San Sisto Vecchio as open daily 9.00 to 12.00 and 16.00 to 18.00, adding that times may vary and advising a telephone call first. The basilica of San Giovanni a Porta Latina states on its own site that it is open every day from 06.30 to 18.00. For the Case Romane del Celio, Roma Capitale publishes the hours as 10.00 to 16.00 Monday to Sunday and on public holidays, with the ticket office closing an hour earlier; closed 1 January and 25 December; 10.00 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December, with booking through Coopculture on 06 39967755.

Two things need planning and three are shut. The Aula Gotica of the Santi Quattro Coronati opens on sixteen published days in 2026 with timed entries and is booked by email in advance, and its site states that the thirteenth-century cloister and the Oratorio di San Silvestro can be visited on those days too, 9.30 to 14.00 and 15.00 to 17.45. The Sepolcro degli Scipioni is entered only by booking on 060608, in groups of no more than twelve with their own guide, or on a published calendar of individual visits. Closed: the Colombario di Pomponio Hylas, which the Sovrintendenza Capitolina states has been temporarily closed to the public since 1 August 2024 for works under the PNRR; the Ninfeo dell'Uccelliera in Villa Celimontana, which Roma Capitale gives as closed to the public; and the Semenzaio di San Sisto, which Roma Capitale states is not open to the public and may be visited only on guided visits of the Dipartimento Ambiente.

faq.question: Is the Colosseum in Celio?
faq.answer: Yes. The amphitheatre stands in Celio, and it is written on this page and on no other page in this series. Its address is Piazza del Colosseo, 00184 Roma. The Arch of Constantine and the ruins of the Meta Sudans are a separate question: Roma Capitale addresses the arch to via di San Gregorio, which the rione's delimitation names as the line with Campitelli, and neither is written here.

faq.question: What are the Colosseum's opening hours, and where do I buy a ticket?
faq.answer: No current opening hours are given here. Times and last admission change with the season; the Parco archeologico del Colosseo publishes them at colosseo.it, and tickets are sold at ticketing.colosseo.it.

faq.question: What is the Museo della Forma Urbis?
faq.answer: A museum in the Parco archeologico del Celio holding the surviving fragments of the Severan marble plan of Rome, incised on 150 slabs of marble between 203 and 211 AD and displayed on the wall of a hall in the Temple of Peace. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the complete plan covered about 18 by 13 metres and represented at least 13,550,000 square metres of city at an average scale of about 1:240. The plan is known from the fragments that survive; they amount to about a tenth of the original. In the museum they lie on the floors, superimposed on Giovanni Battista Nolli's Pianta Grande of 1748.

faq.question: Can you get into the Aula Gotica at the Santi Quattro Coronati?
faq.answer: Only on published days, and only by booking. The site's own calendar for 2026 gives Friday 23 and Saturday 24 January; Friday 6 and Saturday 7 February; Friday 24 and Saturday 25 April; Tuesday 12 and Wednesday 13 May; Friday 12 and Saturday 13 June; Friday 18 and Saturday 19 September; Friday 23 and Saturday 24 October; and Friday 13 and Saturday 14 November, with entry at 09.00, 10.00, 11.00, 12.00, 13.00, 15.00, 16.00, 17.00 and 18.00. Booking is by email to archeocontesti@gmail.com, leaving a telephone contact. The same page states that on those days the thirteenth-century cloister and the Oratorio di San Silvestro may also be visited, 9.30 to 14.00 and 15.00 to 17.45, and that in 2026 the cloister may also be visited on Wednesday and Friday mornings, 9.30 to 11.45, except on holidays. An offering is appreciated for entry.

faq.question: Is anything in Celio free to walk into?
faq.answer: Yes. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives free entry to the Parco archeologico del Celio, with its garden of epigraphic and architectural finds arranged in thematic groups. Villa Celimontana is a public park of 110,000 square metres, open from dawn to sunset, approximately 7.00 to 18.00 from 1 May to 31 October and 7.00 to 17.00 from 1 November to 30 April, and the obelisk of Ramesses II and the Fontana del Fiume stand inside it. The Parco degli Scipioni opens 7.00 to sunset. The fountain of the Navicella on piazza della Navicella, the Fontana di via di San Gregorio and the Arco di Dolabella e Silano all stand in the open street.

faq.question: Why isn't Santo Stefano Rotondo al Celio on this page?
faq.answer: Because a dedication is not an address. Via di Santo Stefano Rotondo is named in the rione's own delimitation as part of the line with Monti, and the basilica is written under Monti in this series, as are San Clemente al Laterano, San Giovanni in Laterano and the park of Colle Oppio. The same caution applies at the other end of the rione: viale delle Terme di Caracalla clips Celio's southern boundary, but the Baths of Caracalla stand in San Saba.

places.name: Colosseo (Anfiteatro Flavio)
places.address: Piazza del Colosseo, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The Flavian amphitheatre, on the western edge of the Caelian. Roma Capitale's tourism office gives it as 189 metres long and 156 metres wide, over 48 metres high, covering 24,000 square metres and able to hold about 50,000 spectators, with an arena of 76 by 46 metres. Four superimposed architectural orders rise on the outside, the lower three of eighty arcades each. No current opening hours are given here. Times and last admission change with the season; the Parco archeologico del Colosseo publishes them at colosseo.it, and tickets are sold at ticketing.colosseo.it.
places.history: The Parco archeologico del Colosseo records that the building, called the Colosseo after a colossal statue, was raised in the first century AD at the wish of the emperors of the Flavian dynasty; Roma Capitale gives construction as begun in 70 AD under Vespasian and completed in 80 AD under Titus. A fire in 217 destroyed the timber-and-rope hoist machinery in the hypogeum. In 438, with the abolition of the gladiatorial games at the wish of Valentinian III, the amphitheatre went into a slow decline, so much so that in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance it was worked as a quarry for materials, some of them used in building the basilica of Saint Peter.

places.name: Museo del Colosseo
places.address: Piazza del Colosseo, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The Parco archeologico del Colosseo's museum, laid out on the second level of the amphitheatre itself and reached on the visit to the monument.
places.history: The Parco archeologico del Colosseo describes the museum in sections: the architecture of the building, how the amphitheatre worked, the gladiator's trade and the venationes, the spectators and the inscribed senatorial loca, the monument's sculptural apparatus, the medieval Colosseum and its Christianisation, the views made by Grand Tour travellers, the Lucangeli model, and the monument's ideological reuse under the regime.

places.name: Piazza del Colosseo
places.address: Piazza del Colosseo, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The open ground around the amphitheatre, which carries the postal address of the Colosseum and of the Museo del Colosseo inside it: Piazza del Colosseo, 00184 Roma.
places.history: The Parco archeologico del Colosseo publishes the public transport serving the square as Metro line B, station Colosseo; buses 51, 75, 81, 85, 87 and 118; and tram 3.

places.name: Parco archeologico del Celio
places.address: Viale del Parco del Celio 20, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A public park on the north-west shoulder of the Caelian facing the Colosseum, with the Museo della Forma Urbis and the Casina del Salvi inside it. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives three entrances — Viale del Parco del Celio 20, Viale del Parco del Celio 22 and Clivo di Scauro 4 — free entry, and opening from 7.00 to 17.30 in winter and 7.00 to 20.00 in summer, closed on 25 December and 1 May. Its information line is 060608, 09.00 to 19.00 daily. The Sovrintendenza states that the archaeological area and the museum are accessible to all. The garden displays epigraphic and architectural finds from the excavations of the late nineteenth century, arranged in thematic groups.
places.history: Roma Capitale gives the sequence: the Cornovaglia family held the ground as a vineyard from the sixteenth century; under the Napoleonic administration the French dumped spoil from the Forum and Colosseum excavations here, producing the artificial terrace; in 1835 Gregory XVI turned the resulting garden into a passeggiata pubblica and Gaspare Salvi laid the avenues and built the Casina; in 1847 both Casina and park passed to the Comune by Motu Proprio of Pius IX. The Ex Antiquarium Comunale went up from 1884 in the northern part and the Ex Palestra della GIL was completed in 1929 in the south. Viale del Parco del Celio, which carried the post-war tram line, divides the park in two.

places.name: Museo della Forma Urbis
places.address: Viale del Parco del Celio 20, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A museum in the Parco archeologico del Celio, housed in the Ex Palestra della Gioventù Italiana del Littorio, holding the surviving fragments of the Severan marble plan of Rome. The fragments lie on the museum floors, superimposed on Giovanni Battista Nolli's Pianta Grande of 1748. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday, 10.00 to 16.00 in winter with last entry at 15.00 and 10.00 to 19.00 in summer with last entry at 18.00, closed on Mondays, 25 December and 1 May. Tickets are sold through the Musei in Comune ticketing service.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the plan was incised on 150 slabs of marble between 203 and 211 AD, under Septimius Severus, and displayed on the wall of a hall in the Temple of Peace, later absorbed into the complex of Santi Cosma e Damiano; the slabs were pinned to the wall with iron dowels. Complete, it covered a surface of about 18 by 13 metres and represented at least 13,550,000 square metres of city, at an average scale of about 1:240. The plan is known from the fragments that survive; they amount to about a tenth of the original. Only about 200 fragments have been identified and placed on modern topography. Fragments were found from 1562 onward; Roma Capitale records that the plan entered the Capitoline collections in 1742, that the last comprehensive arrangement of the originals was in the garden of the Palazzo dei Conservatori between 1903 and 1924, and that until 1939 significant groups were visible in the Antiquarium del Celio.

places.name: Casina del Salvi
places.address: Viale del Parco del Celio 20, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A caffetteria in the Parco archeologico del Celio, with the bar on the ground floor and the outside terrace and a study room upstairs, fitted with wi-fi, tables with charging points and space to sit. Roma Capitale gives the opening as every day, 9.00 to 16.30 in winter and 9.00 to 19.00 in summer.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the Casina was built in 1835 against the remains of the Temple of the Deified Claudius, at the wish of Gregory XVI, as a caffetteria, and that it is named for its architect Gaspare Salvi, who took Valadier's coffee-house on the Pincio as his model. After restoration it returned to its nineteenth-century use.

places.name: Ex Antiquarium Comunale del Celio
places.summary: The former municipal antiquarium in the northern part of the Parco archeologico del Celio. It is closed and has been since 1939. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes a recovery project for the building under the PNRR – Caput Mundi programme.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the building was conceived from 1882 to house the finds from the excavations that followed the proclamation of Rome as capital, and designed by Costantino Sneider as a Museo Urbano e Magazzino Archeologico. The first six rooms of the Magazzino Archeologico were inaugurated in 1889 and a seventh in 1906. From 1925 Antonio Muñoz was given the enlargement, completed in 1929, which turned it into a museum of the minor arts while the major sculpture went to the Palazzo dei Conservatori. In 1938 Muñoz added three superimposed rooms on the east side, completed early in 1939; a few months later, work on building the metropolitana tunnel caused significant structural problems, leading on 5 December of that year to a closure that proved to be permanent.

places.name: Tempio del Divo Claudio (resti)
places.summary: The remains of the temple to the deified Claudius, on the western slope of the Caelian, which the Sovrintendenza Capitolina records under Rione XIX - Celio. Nothing of the temple building itself survives, but the substructures of its platform stand substantially, notably on the east side along the modern via Claudia. On the west side a series of two-storey rooms with a travertine façade survives inside the property of the church and convent of Santi Giovanni e Paolo. The Museo della Forma Urbis stands on the same platform.
places.history: Claudius died in 54 AD and was deified. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the temple is known only from a fragment of the Severan marble plan, the Forma Urbis: prostyle and hexastyle, fronting north, raised on a rectangular platform of 180 by 200 metres. Nero built a monumental nymphaeum against that flank as a backdrop to the Domus Aurea and destroyed the temple, which Vespasian rebuilt.

places.name: Basilica dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo al Celio
places.address: Piazza dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo 13, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A titular basilica on the Clivo di Scauro, held by the Passionists, with the Case Romane del Celio beneath it. Roma Capitale publishes the basilica's hours as 08.30–12.45 and 14.00–17.00, with the note that some times may vary during the wedding season. The rector receives on Wednesday, Thursday and Saturday, 09.00 to 12.00 and 15.30 to 17.00. Mass with the people is at 11.45 on Sundays and feasts from the first Sunday of September, celebrated in the Cappella di San Paolo della Croce.
places.history: The basilica's own account says it was raised from 398 by the senator Byzantius or by his son Pammachius, on the site of a building of the first or second century used first as a domus ecclesiae, and that it is first cited in the acts of a synod held by Pope Symmachus in 499 as Titulus Pammachii or Titulus Byzantii. It was damaged by Alaric's Visigoths in the sack of 410 and by an earthquake in 442, and sacked by the Normans in 1084; Paschal II, pope from 1099 to 1118, promoted the restoration and added the campanile and the portico. Roma Capitale records that it was rebuilt from the foundations in the twelfth century, the tall campanile set on the remains of the Temple of Claudius, and that in 1216 Cardinal Cencio Savelli, the future Honorius III, raised the portico to create the gallery above it and the Cosmatesque portal with an eagle and two lions. Substantial work followed in 1715 under Cardinal Fabrizio Paolucci, and the Romanesque façade was reinstated between 1950 and 1952 at the wish of Cardinal Francis Joseph Spellman. The ceiling is coffered, of the sixteenth century; a large Pomarancio fresco fills the apse; and a slab about halfway down the nave marks the place where the saints were martyred in aedibus propriis.

places.name: Casa di esercizi per il clero dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo
places.summary: The Clergy Retreat House of Sts John and Paul stands in Celio, on Italian soil, and is named in Article 16 of the 1929 Lateran Treaty. No source states any visiting arrangement, so none is given here.
places.history: Article 16 provides that the buildings it names will never be subject to liens or to expropriation for reasons of public utility save by previous agreement with the Holy See, and will be exempt from taxes, whether ordinary or extraordinary. The Treaty's Article 15, which grants the immunities of the headquarters of diplomatic agents of foreign States, applies to a different list of properties and does not name this one.

places.name: Case Romane del Celio
places.address: Clivo di Scauro, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: Twenty finely frescoed underground rooms beneath the basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, dated between the first and the fourth century, entered from the Clivo di Scauro, which Roma Capitale describes as an ancient Roman road and the principal axis of the Caelian, keeping part of its original course. Roma Capitale publishes the hours as 10.00–16.00 Monday to Sunday and on public holidays, with the ticket office closing an hour earlier; closed 1 January and 25 December; 10.00–14.00 on 24 and 31 December. Booking through Coopculture on 06 39967755.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the rooms were discovered in 1887 by Padre Germano di San Stanislao, then rector of the basilica, and that they show a sequence of buildings on one site: a two-level domus with a private balneum of the early second century, an insula with street-level tabernae of the early third, a luxurious domus of the late third to early fourth, and a titulus of the middle of the fourth century.

places.name: Chiesa di San Gregorio al Celio
places.address: Piazza di San Gregorio 1, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The church of Gregory the Great's own monastery, served by the Camaldolese, reached up a broad staircase from via di San Gregorio. Roma Capitale's page for it publishes Mass times only. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. The community's telephone number is 06 7008227.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Gregory, who came from the Anicii and had been Praefectus Urbis, founded the monastery in 575 by turning his family house over to it, and that of the medieval building only the thirteenth-century Cosmatesque pavement survives. The complex was granted in 1573 to the Camaldolese, who still serve it. The staircase and the square in front were rebuilt for the Jubilee of 1600, and in 1633 Cardinal Scipione Borghese gave Giovanni Battista Soria the atrium and the façade, which carry the Borghese eagle and dragons. Roma Capitale records that the portico holds the tomb of Sir Edward Carne, sent to Rome by Henry VIII in 1561 over the divorce from Catherine of Aragon. The interior has three naves on sixteen antique columns and is baroque after Francesco Ferrari's work of 1725; a small chapel off the right aisle holds Gregory's marble episcopal seat, of the first century BC; and the Cappella Salviati, by Francesco da Volterra and completed by Carlo Maderno in 1600, holds the fresco of the Madonna con Bambino.

places.name: Oratori di Sant'Andrea, Santa Silvia e Santa Barbara al Celio
places.address: Piazza di San Gregorio, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: Three free-standing chapels in the garden of the church of San Gregorio al Celio. No source states their opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the Cappella di Sant'Andrea, in the centre, holds frescoes by Domenichino and by Guido Reni, and that Reni also painted the apse Concerto degli Angeli in the Cappella di Santa Silvia. The Cappella di Santa Barbara contains the Triclinio, the marble table at which Gregory served lunch to twelve poor men; in memory of it, every Maundy Thursday until 1870 the pope served lunch here to thirteen poor men.

places.name: Parco di San Gregorio al Celio
places.address: Salita di San Gregorio 3, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A park of 1.9 hectares on the western slope of the Caelian, formed out of the old kitchen garden of the monastery of San Gregorio and reached by a stair from the salita di San Gregorio lined with olives. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places it in Municipio I, Rione XIX - Celio, and gives its bounds as Villa Celimontana to the east, the Semenzaio Comunale to the south, via Valle delle Camene to the west and the conventual complex of Santi Andrea e Gregorio Magno to the north. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina relates the original settlement to the palace or villa of Gordianus, father of Gregory the Great, which Gregory turned into a hermitage around 580. The first monastery had, as well as the church and the oratory to St Andrew, a library, a guest house, a granary and a stable. It passed to Greek Basilian monks in the eighth century, back to the Benedictines in the first half of the tenth, and definitively to the Camaldolese in 1573. Surviving service buildings include a medieval house restructured in the late fifteenth century, a small casale that is now the park keeper's lodge, and a former vaccheria.

places.name: Fontana di via di San Gregorio
places.address: Via di San Gregorio, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A fountain set into the retaining wall of the Antiquarium on the slope of the Caelian, framed by two massive brick propylaea. The vertical element is a marble saracinesca over which the water runs as a cascade into a rectangular serpentine basin with recesses on two sides, approached by three travertine steps between travertine corner posts; on the back wall are two marble tablets that originally carried fasces, later chiselled off, and S.P.Q.R. in relief capitals. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records it under Rione Celio and gives the author as Antonio Muñoz, the date as 1933, and the materials as white marble, serpentine, travertine and peperino.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places the fountain in the wider rearrangement that accompanied the reopening of the Antiquarium in 1929 and the widening of the road — then via dei Trionfi, now via di San Gregorio — from the Arch of Constantine to piazzale di Porta Capena, under the master plan of 1931.

places.name: Villa Celimontana
places.address: Via della Navicella, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A public park of 110,000 square metres on the Caelian, what remains of the Mattei garden, with entrances on via della Navicella and on piazza dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places it in Municipio I, Rione XIX - Celio and dates it to the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries. Roma Capitale gives the opening as from dawn to sunset, approximately 7.00 to 18.00 from 1 May to 31 October and 7.00 to 17.00 from 1 November to 30 April.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the land around Santa Maria in Domnica was bought in the mid 1500s by Giacomo Mattei and given in dowry to his daughter Claudia, wife and cousin of Ciriaco Mattei, who turned the vineyard into a garden of statues and fountains. Work probably began in 1572, the casino from after 1577 and probably finished by 1581, traditionally begun by Jacopo Del Duca, a pupil of Michelangelo. The hanging garden and the teatro were laid out as an antique circus with a tiered hemicycle, with the Egyptian obelisk as its spina. The villa stayed with the Mattei until the male line died out in the early nineteenth century. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that in 1926 the Palazzina Mattei passed to the Regia Società Geografica Italiana and the park was designated public green space, opened to the public in 1928. Roma Capitale adds that the villa covers a Flavian and Trajanic site with enclosure walls partly visible, that the castra of the fifth cohort of the Vigiles stood here, and that excavations of the late 1800s brought up the Basilica Hilariana.

places.name: Palazzetto Mattei in Villa Celimontana (Società Geografica Italiana)
places.address: Via della Navicella 12, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The Mattei casino inside Villa Celimontana, which has housed the Società Geografica Italiana, founded in Florence in 1867, since 1926. Roma Capitale gives its library as about 400,000 volumes on geography and allied disciplines with a rare-books section running from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century, a Cartoteca of about 200,000 maps including Chinese and Japanese maps of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, mostly manuscript, a Historical Archive of letters, travel notebooks and explorers' drawings, and a Photographic Archive of about 400,000 phototypes. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the Palazzetto was built to a design by Jacopo Del Duca for Ciriaco Mattei, who commissioned the architect in 1580 for the building and for the first laying out of the park. Ciriaco's son Gian Battista turned it from a home for the collection into a private residence and extended the gardens, with Francesco Peparelli finishing the work in 1623; the Library frescoes on mythological subjects, by Pietro Sigismondi, Orazio Monaldi and Orazio Zecca, date from then. A third-century Roman mosaic, found in front of the building during a nineteenth-century restoration, is displayed inside.

places.name: Obelisco Mattejano (Obelisco Capitolino)
places.summary: An Egyptian obelisk standing in the garden of Villa Celimontana, the twin of the one on piazza della Rotonda. Roma Capitale gives the original height as about 7 metres, of which only the upper section of about 3 metres survives; the lower part was never recovered. It is crowned by a bronze ball said by some to have held the ashes of Octavian.
places.history: The surviving upper section carries hieroglyphs naming Ramesses II and came from Heliopolis. It stood on the Campidoglio beside the stair to the convent of Santa Maria in Aracoeli before Ciriaco Mattei obtained it from the Comune and set it in his villa, where it stands in the garden. Roma Capitale records that on the Campidoglio four lions at the corners of the base supported the shaft, that the obelisk fell and was carried off and forgotten, and that Ciriaco Mattei found it again at the end of the 1500s. His heirs left villa and obelisk neglected, and the next owner, Manuel de Godoy, formerly Spanish first minister in the Napoleonic period, saw to its conservation.

places.name: Ninfeo dell'Uccelliera di Villa Celimontana
places.summary: An underground chamber of the late sixteenth century, built during work on the villa's western slopes between 1585 and 1590, beneath the aviary that stood to the right of the casino nobile until it was destroyed in the eighteenth century. Roma Capitale gives it as closed to the public.
places.history: Roma Capitale describes a stair rising from the avenue between landings paved in polychrome mosaic showing an eagle, the Mattei heraldic device. The apsed nymphaeum has a lower band faced in tartari — marble chips, pumice cubes and calcareous concretions set as mosaic in geometric modules — and an upper zone of coloured plaster with multicoloured marble fragments and groups of shells, with grotesque figures in the central zone; masonry seats faced in peperino run round the apse. In 1613 a sculptor recorded only as Battista made a triton on a sea horse for a fountain here, removed in the eighteenth century when the nymphaeum became a shaded resting place.

places.name: Fontana del Fiume a Villa Celimontana
places.summary: A seventeenth-century fountain in Villa Celimontana commissioned by Ciriaco Mattei: an elliptical basin backed by a masonry architectural screen with two open niches, surmounted by a semi-reclining marble statue, possibly a personification of the river Nera, holding a skin from which the water flows.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the statue's head, stolen in 2005, was recovered and put back in its place in 2007.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Domnica alla Navicella
places.address: Via della Navicella 10, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica facing the fountain of the Navicella, with a five-arched portico and a ninth-century apse mosaic. The parish gives Mass at 19.00 Monday to Friday, 19.00 on Saturday, and 11.00 and 19.00 on Sunday.
places.history: Roma Capitale records an ancient diaconia, probably founded in the seventh century on the Roman remains of the barracks of the fifth cohort of the Vigiles. The epithet in Domnica is of uncertain origin: possibly from the name Ciriaca, from dominicum for early Christian places of worship, or from the praedia dominica. The present appearance is largely due to Paschal I, who rebuilt the church from the foundations in the ninth century and decorated it with the apse mosaic, in which he appears at the Virgin's feet among ranks of angels. Between 1513 and 1514 the titular cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, the future Leo X, had the façade rebuilt to a design by Andrea Sansovino, who also designed the portico of five arches on piers and Tuscan pilasters with lion protomes alluding to the pope's chosen name. The campanile on the right flank keeps a thirteenth-century bell. The plan is basilican, three naves on eighteen antique granite columns with Corinthian capitals; the coffered wooden ceiling was made in 1565 and 1566 for Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici, with a heraldic frieze below it designed by Giulio Romano; the frescoes under the mosaic are of the seventeenth century.

places.name: Fontana della Navicella
places.address: Piazza della Navicella, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A marble ship set as a fountain on piazza della Navicella, in front of Santa Maria in Domnica. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records it under Rione Celio, attributes it to Andrea Sansovino, and gives the materials as white marble and travertine. The ship rests on two thole-pins; the deck has a handrail on nine corbels alternating with nine hatches; the stern carries a castle; and Roma Capitale describes the protome carved on the prow as a boar's head. The floor of the basin is a river-pebble mosaic with fish and boats.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the first mention of a navicella here is of 1484, by Pomponio Leto, and refers to an earlier sculpture, perhaps Roman, and that the present sculpture was made in 1518 and 1519 for Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, presumably by Sansovino, who had restored the church for the same cardinal in 1513 and 1514. It was adapted as a fountain in 1931 during the widening of the road, when its orientation was changed and a low elliptical basin was made at its base; from that year it was fed from a secondary branch of the Acqua Felice. The prow now faces the historic centre with the sides parallel to the church portico, where it once stood with the stern towards the portico. Roma Capitale reports a legend that makes the little ship an ex-voto to Isis from sailors of the Castra Peregrinorum or the Castra Misenantium, the Misenum fleet sailors quartered on the Caelian who worked the Colosseum's velarium. The fountain was restored in 2003 and 2004; in September 2005 an act of vandalism detached and removed the animal protome, and the recovered pieces were reassembled.

places.name: Basilica Hilariana
places.address: Largo della Sanità Militare, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A Roman complex of the middle of the second century AD, standing inside the grounds of the Policlinico Militare del Celio, identified as a place of worship of Cybele and Attis and as the seat of the religious college of the dendrophori. No source states its visiting arrangements, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the building was discovered at the end of the 1800s and largely excavated in the following century, and that an inscription on a statue base and a portrait head found inside show it was built by Manius Publicius Hilarus, a wealthy pearl merchant and follower of the cult of Cybele. A central courtyard is preceded by an entrance vestibule giving on to further rooms, with an upper floor that no longer stands; the vestibule mosaic shows animals round a human eye pierced by a lance, apotropaic in function. In the third century a shrine was built for the pine sacred to Attis, the Arbor Sancta. From the fourth century some of the service rooms were given over to production, and the building was abandoned between the fifth and sixth centuries.

places.name: Chiesa di San Tommaso in Formis
places.address: Via di San Paolo della Croce 10, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A church dedicated to Thomas the Apostle, whose name in Formis comes, Roma Capitale writes, from the Latin name of the Claudian aqueduct — forma Claudia — on whose cisterns it was built. Over the door is a mosaic of Christ between two freed slaves, one white and one black, the emblem of the Trinitarian order. Visits and Mass times are arranged through the Curia Generalizia of the Order; the telephone numbers Roma Capitale gives are 06 35420529 and 06 52725090.
places.history: Roma Capitale binds the church to the Order of the Most Holy Trinity and its founder John of Matha, who spent his last years probably in the cell behind the little window above the Arch of Dolabella and Silanus and died on 17 December 1213; his remains were first entombed in a marble mausoleum in the church and were moved to Spain in 1655. The church was built around the tenth century as the abbey church of a Benedictine monastery, though the date cannot be fixed because the written record was destroyed. The first attestations are of 1209, when Innocent III gave the existing monastery to the Trinitarians, who made it their seat and adapted part of it as a hospital for the poor, the sick, pilgrims and slaves ransomed by the order. Around 1380, under Urban VI, the order had to leave Rome for supporting the antipope Clement VII, and the Vatican Chapter took the complex and closed the hospital. In 1532 the church was restored using material from the hospital to save money. In 1571 Pius V returned the church and what was left of hospital and monastery to the Trinitarians, who lost them again at his death months later. A restoration of 1663 gave the church its façade, with a portal under a triangular tympanum inscribed DIVO THOMAE APOST(OLO) D(ICATUM). The complex went back to the Trinitarians in 1898 and the church reopened for worship in 1926, the hospital by then demolished.

places.name: Arco di Dolabella e Silano (Porta Caelimontana)
places.address: Via di San Paolo della Croce, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A gate of the Servian Walls, rebuilt by Augustus and identified with the Porta Caelimontana, later used to carry Nero's aqueduct across the street. Roma Capitale gives it as 4 metres in width and 6.56 metres in height, with part of it now below ground, and records the monument under Rione XIX - Celio.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the arch was built at the start of the first century AD by the consuls Dolabella and Silanus, per the inscription on the attic: P. CORNELIS P. F. DOLABELLA C. IUNIUS C. F. SILANUS FLAMEN MARTIAL(is) CO(n)S(ules) EX S(enatus) C(onsulto) FACIUNDUM CURAVERUNT IDEMQUE PROBAVER(unt). It was rebuilt with travertine blocks over the original tufa blocks, which are still visible in the right-hand wall. Tradition places John of Matha in the room above it from 1209 until his death in 1213. Roma Capitale records that the Caelian was anciently called Mons Querquetulanus, because it was covered in oaks.

places.name: Basilica e Complesso dei Santi Quattro Coronati
places.address: Via dei Santi Quattro 20, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A fortified medieval complex on the Caelian: the basilica, the monks' cells, the cloister and the cardinal's palace, whose entrance is dominated by the Torre Maggiore. Enclosed Augustinian nuns live here. The monastery publishes a summer timetable of prayer: on weekdays Lauds at 07.45, Terce at 08.30, Vespers at 18.30 and Mass at 19.00; on Saturday Mass with Lauds at 07.45 and the Rosary and Vespers at 18.00; on Sundays and solemnities Lauds at 08.00, Terce at 08.45, Sext at 10.45, Mass at 11.00 and Vespers with Eucharistic Adoration at 18.00. Telephone 06 70475427.
places.history: Roma Capitale records a foundation in the middle of the fifth century AD on the remains of a Roman domus, named from the tradition of the martyrdom of four Roman soldiers and five stonemasons. The complex was entirely rebuilt after the fire that devastated the city in 1084, and at the start of the thirteenth century the monks' cells, the cloister and the fortified cardinal's palace were added. Decline set in with the move of the papacy to Avignon and lasted until 1564, when Pius IV turned the complex into the Conservatorio delle Zitelle, a girls' orphanage, for the enclosed Augustinian nuns. The interior has three naves under matronea, on columns taken from imperial monuments, and keeps its original Cosmatesque pavement of large marble and porphyry discs and polychrome mosaic. The apse spans all three naves, covering the width of the nave of the first basilica, and is frescoed by Giovanni da San Giovanni with the story of the Coronati.

places.name: Chiostro e Oratorio di San Silvestro, Santi Quattro Coronati
places.address: Via dei Santi Quattro 20, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: The thirteenth-century cloister and the Cappella di San Silvestro, the oratory of the cardinal's palace, inside the complex of the Santi Quattro Coronati. Roma Capitale gives the Oratorio di San Silvestro as visitable Monday to Saturday, 09.30 to 12.00, and states that the afternoon opening, Monday to Sunday 16.00 to 17.30, is not guaranteed. The Aula Gotica's own site states that during its public openings the thirteenth-century cloister and the Oratorio di San Silvestro may also be visited, 9.30 to 14.00 and 15.00 to 17.45, and that in 2026 the cloister may also be visited on Wednesday and Friday mornings, 9.30 to 11.45, except on holidays; an offering is appreciated for entry.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that from the Stanza del Calendario, the antechamber to the nuns' parlour, which carries a thirteenth-century fresco, one reaches the Cappella di San Silvestro, painted with the Stories of Pope Sylvester, among them the Donation of Constantine.

places.name: Aula Gotica dei Santi Quattro Coronati
places.address: Via dei Santi Quattro 20, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A hall in the cardinal's palace of the Santi Quattro Coronati whose walls and vaults carry 300 square metres of thirteenth-century painting, which Roma Capitale suggests may have been the courtroom of an ecclesiastical tribunal; the profane scenes are by the Terzo Maestro di Anagni. Its own site gives the 2026 opening days as Friday 23 and Saturday 24 January; Friday 6 and Saturday 7 February; Friday 24 and Saturday 25 April; Tuesday 12 and Wednesday 13 May; Friday 12 and Saturday 13 June; Friday 18 and Saturday 19 September; Friday 23 and Saturday 24 October; and Friday 13 and Saturday 14 November, with entry at 09.00, 10.00, 11.00, 12.00, 13.00, 15.00, 16.00, 17.00 and 18.00. Booking is by email to archeocontesti@gmail.com, leaving a telephone contact.
places.history: The paintings were uncovered in 1995 beneath later layers of colour and brought back by a long restoration carried out by the state Soprintendenze.

places.name: Sepolcro degli Scipioni
places.address: Via di Porta San Sebastiano 9, Roma RM
places.summary: The tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones, in an archaeological area on the urban stretch of the via Appia Antica, inside the Aurelian Walls before the Porta San Sebastiano. Roma Capitale states that entry is allowed to groups and associations with their own guide, who must book on 060608, daily 9.00 to 19.00, with a maximum of 12 people per visit; individual visits are booked on the same number to a published calendar.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the monumental tomb was built in the first decades of the third century BC by Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus, whose sarcophagus stood facing the entrance, and that the via Appia had been inaugurated in 312 BC. The first notice of a discovery is of 1614 and the area was re-excavated in 1780; everything inscribed or figured went to the Vatican Museums. Between 1926 and 1929 the Comune ran a campaign of excavation, restoration and arrangement to open the area, which included laying out the Parco degli Scipioni behind it towards the via Latina. Roma Capitale describes the structure as quadrangular in plan, with a monumental entrance now almost entirely gone and six galleries cut in the tufa, sarcophagi set along the walls or in niches, each with its inscription.

places.name: Parco degli Scipioni
places.address: Via di Porta Latina 10, Roma RM
places.summary: A park of 16,000 square metres between the ancient via Latina and the via Appia, now via di Porta San Sebastiano, inside the Aurelian circuit. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places it in Municipio I, Rione XIX - Celio, dates it 1928 to 1931, gives its entrances as Via di Porta Latina 10 and Via di Porta San Sebastiano, the latter currently closed, and gives the opening as 7.00 to sunset. A long central avenue runs from the via di Porta Latina entrance across the park, with tall pines and cypresses and Mediterranean planting — holm oak, laurel, myrtle — flanking the remains.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes the park as the result of an archaeological arrangement that recovered the Colombario di Pomponio Hylas and the Sepolcro degli Scipioni, with the garden designed by Raffaele de Vico, who finished in 1931. From the seventeenth century the ground had been vineyards and kitchen gardens. In 1831 Pietro Campana discovered the Colombario di Pomponio Hylas, and from 1840 three columbaria were uncovered in the adjoining Vigna Codini. The Comune bought the archaeological zone after unification, and the X Ripartizione Antichità e Belle Arti began the full restoration of the Sepolcro in 1926.

places.name: Colombario di Pomponio Hylas
places.address: Via di Porta Latina 10, Roma RM
places.summary: A painted underground burial chamber inside the Parco degli Scipioni, which the Sovrintendenza Capitolina records under Rione XIX - Celio. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that the site has been temporarily closed to the public since 1 August 2024 for works under the PNRR. The conditions it publishes for when the site reopens are: full entry 4.00 euro, reduced 3.00 euro; free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and for MIC card holders; groups accompanied, a maximum of 7 people per visit, booking obligatory on 060608, 09.00 to 19.00.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina places the columbarium on a side road off the ancient via Latina and records that it was discovered in 1831 by the Marchese Pietro Campana. It is named from the freedman Pomponius Hylas, whose funerary inscription, a tablet in glass-paste mosaic, is above the stair down to the burial chamber. Other inscriptions place the construction between the principate of Tiberius and that of Claudius, 14 to 51 AD, with continued use in the Flavian period, 69 to 96, when the Hylas mosaic and some decorative changes are dated, down to the Antonine age, 138 to 161. A steep stair leads into a rectangular room under a vault finely decorated with plant motifs; the niches for the ash-jars sit in small aedicular structures with colonnettes and tympana, painted and stuccoed. In the central aedicule of the end wall two figures are painted, probably the tomb's founders, named on the marble tablet below as Granius Nestor and Vinileia Hedone. The figurative programme centres on Orpheus.

places.name: Basilica di San Giovanni a Porta Latina
places.address: Via di Porta Latina 17, 00179 Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica preceded by a forecourt shaded by a large cedar. Its own site states that it is in the pastoral care of the Istituto della Carità, the Rosminian Fathers, and that the basilica is open every day from 06.30 to 18.00. The summer Mass timetable published by the basilica gives weekdays at 07.30 in the college chapel, Saturday at 07.30, and Sundays and holy days of obligation at 11.30. Telephone 06 70475938; email portalatina17@gmail.com.
places.history: Roma Capitale records a foundation probably in the fifth century, which roof tiles with stamps of the Theodoric period seem to attest, a rebuilding at the end of the eighth century and a restoration in 1191. The dedication is to John the Evangelist, who by tradition survived the attempted martyrdom in boiling oil at the Porta Latina. The portico has five arches and keeps inside it the original Borrominian finial of San Giovanni in Oleo. The Romanesque campanile on the left is of the twelfth century, square, of five orders, with triple-light openings on colonnettes in the upper three. In the courtyard a ninth-century well stands between two columns with fourth-century capitals, inscribed round the mouth with the baptismal formula and the words EGO STEFANUS. The interior has three naves on two rows of five columns of differing marble, and the twelfth-century fresco cycle on the central nave, found during the restoration of 1940, shows 46 different scenes from the Old and New Testaments.

places.name: Oratorio di San Giovanni in Oleo
places.address: Via di Porta Latina 77, 00179 Roma RM
places.summary: A small octagonal oratory of the start of the sixteenth century, perhaps built over an ancient pagan mausoleum whose circular form it echoes. Roma Capitale gives it as visitable on request, applying to the church of San Giovanni a Porta Latina.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the design is attributed variously to Bramante, to Antonio da Sangallo the Younger and to Baldassarre Peruzzi, and that the oratory was built at the expense of the French prelate Benedetto Adam, recorded on one of the two doors with the motto Au plaisir de Dieu. In 1658 Cardinal Francesco Paolucci had it restored along with San Giovanni a Porta Latina, of which he was titular, and the work went to Francesco Borromini, who altered the covering with a drum, a tall stucco frieze and a conical roof ending in a sheaf of leaves under a globe decorated with roses, alluding to the Paolucci arms. In 1967 the finial was replaced by a plaster cast and the original was placed under the portico of San Giovanni a Porta Latina, where it still is. The walls were decorated at the same time with stuccoes and frescoes attributed to Lazzaro Baldi.

places.name: Parco Egerio
places.address: Piazzale Numa Pompilio, Roma RM
places.summary: A public garden of lawns, tall trees and shrubs on the Caelian slopes, whose planting keeps the green backdrop of the hill as it is seen from the Appia Antica. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the park is named because the legendary lucus camenarum, the Grove of the Camenae, stood on the Caelian slopes outside the walls, with a spring in a grotto where by legend the nymph Egeria met Numa Pompilius, and that classical sources say the grotto was given a monumental marble facing in the imperial period, to the scandal of contemporaries who missed the old grass and tufa.

places.name: Basilica di San Sisto Vecchio
places.address: Piazzale Numa Pompilio 8, Roma RM
places.summary: The church where Dominic de Guzmán founded his first Roman convent, with a twelfth-century campanile and an eighteenth-century façade by Filippo Raguzzini. Roma Capitale gives the church as open every day from 9.00 to 12.00 and from 16.00 to 18.00, adding that the times may be subject to variation and advising visitors to telephone the basilica first, on 06 77205177.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the dedication to Pope Sixtus II, martyred in 258 at the catacombs of San Callisto, appears in a sixth-century document but that the church had been built in the previous century. It was renewed under Innocent III and then entrusted to Dominic de Guzmán, who founded his first Roman convent here; the Dominicans left after two years, moving in 1220 to Santa Sabina, and Dominic used the monastery for his new order of enclosed Dominican nuns, largely drawn from the Tempoline of the monastery of Santa Maria in Tempulo. Church and monastery were restored again under Sixtus IV. At the end of the sixteenth century, the area being malarial, the nuns obtained a move to a new church in Rione Monti, and from then San Sisto was called Vecchio to distinguish it from Santi Domenico e Sisto, called Sisto Nuovo. In the eighteenth century Benedict XIII had the ruinous complex rebuilt by Filippo Raguzzini, who put up the present façade and a new cloister. Since the end of the 1800s the complex has been run by the Congregation of Dominican Sisters founded by Suor Maria Antonia Lalia, and it houses a private school. The interior, once of three naves, is now a single nave decorated in stucco, keeping remains of a late-thirteenth-century fresco cycle between the thirteenth-century apse and the narrower fifteenth-century one; the cloister galleries are painted with Stories of the Life of St Dominic by Andrea Casale, of the eighteenth century.

places.name: Semenzaio di San Sisto
places.address: Via Druso 2, Roma RM
places.summary: The working nursery of Roma Capitale's Servizio Giardini, which has its seat here. Roma Capitale states that the Semenzaio is not open to the public and can be visited only on guided visits organised by the Dipartimento Ambiente. The azaleas that dress the Spanish Steps each April and May are grown here, along with orchids and carnivorous plants.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the story begins in the early 1800s, when Camille de Tournon was made prefect of Rome after the French occupation and had the idea of a pépinière, a nursery to raise the plants for Rome's new avenues and public parks, on the land of the monastery of San Sisto where enclosed Dominican nuns had lived since 1222. A watercourse entering Rome at Porta Metronia fed two water mills, the Mola di San Sisto Vecchio and the Molella, whose structures survive in part. When the French left in 1814 the papal government inherited 30,000 trees ready for transplanting. The nursery was restored in 1926 by the landscape architect Raffaele De Vico, who designed the iron and glass greenhouses and the Aranciera with its neoclassical façade.

places.name: Complesso Vignola Mattei (ex Santa Maria in Tempulo)
places.address: Via di Valle delle Camene, Roma RM
places.summary: A deconsecrated church owned by the Comune di Roma, where civil weddings are now celebrated; Roma Capitale gives it as open on the occasion of wedding ceremonies. Via di Valle delle Camene follows the initial course of the ancient via Appia and takes its name from the spring sacred to the Camenae, from which the Vestals drew the water for their rites.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that a small oratory to St Agatha was built here by a Greek religious community, probably by the end of the sixth century, and that at the start of the ninth the church is linked to a monasterium Tempuli holding a venerated Marian icon. The church under its present dedication, with the attached Benedictine nunnery, is mentioned unambiguously for the first time in 1155, and the campanile, whose remains are now embedded in the external wall, dates from then. In 1222 Dominic moved the Tempoline nuns to San Sisto Vecchio, taking the icon, which is now at Santa Maria del Rosario a Monte Mario. The complex became a private house until, in the seventeenth century, it was absorbed into the Mattei estate of Villa Celimontana and presumably turned into a nymphaeum; Nolli's eighteenth-century plans describe it as a hay barn. It was saved from demolition when the Parco di Porta Capena passeggiata archeologica was created at the start of the twentieth century, and was then given rent-free until the 1980s to sculptors, among them Michele La Spina, Francesco Sansone and Ugo Quaglieri.

places.name: Aurelian Walls, Celio segment
places.summary: The stretch of the Aurelian Walls that forms the south-eastern side of the rione, running from Porta Metronia to Porta San Sebastiano with the quartiere of Appio-Latino beyond it. Roma Capitale gives the whole circuit as about 19 kilometres of brick, with a square tower every thirty metres — a hundred Roman feet — a height of about 6 metres and a thickness of 3.5 metres as first built.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the walls were built between 270 and 275 AD at the wish of Aurelian, that the works, begun in 271, were completed under Probus, emperor from 276 to 282, and that in 401 and 402, under Honorius and Arcadius, the height was doubled and the old wall-walk replaced by covered corridors with a new open crenellated walk above them; further restoration followed in the sixth century under Belisarius. Large existing buildings were absorbed into the circuit, among them the Praetorian camp, the Amphitheatrum Castrense, the Pyramid of Cestius, the Muro Torto and stretches of aqueduct. In 2020 the Comune and Acea installed new lighting on the stretch from piazzale Metronio to via Numidia, 78 recessed projectors and 47 step-markers.

places.name: Hotel Lancelot
places.address: Via Capo d'Africa 47, 00184 Roma RM
places.summary: A hotel on Via Capo d'Africa, which its own site describes as a three-star and places in the Celio. Telephone 06 70450615.

places.name: Pizzeria Li Rioni
places.address: Via dei Santi Quattro 24, Roma RM
places.summary: A pizzeria on Via dei Santi Quattro. The pizzeria says its dough is left to mature for more than eighteen hours and its pizza is baked in a wood-fired oven. It lists Lazio wines. Telephone 06 70450605; info@lirioni.it.

places.name: Naumachia
places.address: Via Celimontana 7, Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on Via Celimontana whose own site gives its cooking as Roman and Tuscan, with carbonara, cacio e pepe and ribollita among the dishes it names. The site is published in Italian, German, Spanish, French, English, Portuguese and Chinese.

places.name: Hostaria i Clementini
places.address: Via di San Giovanni in Laterano 106, Roma RM
places.summary: A hostaria at Via di San Giovanni in Laterano 106, serving Roman cooking. This guide has its name, its address and its kind of cooking and nothing further.

places.name: Osteria il Bocconcino
places.address: Via Ostilia 23, Roma RM
places.summary: An osteria on Via Ostilia serving Roman home cooking. The dishes it names on its own site include zucchine ripiene, tagliolini con ragù d'anatra, fettuccine alla Messisbugo, polpette ebraiche and tordo matto.

entries.name: Colosseo (Anfiteatro Flavio)
entries.note: The Flavian amphitheatre, begun in 70 AD under Vespasian and finished in 80 AD under Titus: 189 by 156 metres, over 48 metres high, with an arena of 76 by 46 metres.

entries.name: Piazza del Colosseo
entries.note: The Parco archeologico del Colosseo gives the square's transport as Metro line B, station Colosseo, buses 51, 75, 81, 85, 87 and 118, and tram 3.

entries.name: Parco archeologico del Celio
entries.note: A free park on the shoulder of the hill facing the Colosseum, open 7.00 to 17.30 in winter and 7.00 to 20.00 in summer, with finds from the excavations of the late nineteenth century set out in the garden.

entries.name: Museo della Forma Urbis
entries.note: The surviving fragments of the Severan marble plan of Rome, incised between 203 and 211 AD, laid out on the museum floors over Nolli's Pianta Grande of 1748.

entries.name: Case Romane del Celio
entries.note: Twenty frescoed underground rooms beneath the basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, found in 1887 and running from a second-century domus to a fourth-century titulus.

entries.name: Basilica dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo al Celio
entries.note: Raised from 398 on the site of a house church, with a campanile set on the remains of the Temple of Claudius; Roma Capitale gives the hours as 08.30 to 12.45 and 14.00 to 17.00.

entries.name: Villa Celimontana
entries.note: The Mattei garden of the late sixteenth century, now a public park of 110,000 square metres, open from dawn to sunset.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Domnica alla Navicella
entries.note: A ninth-century rebuilding by Paschal I, who put himself at the Virgin's feet in the apse mosaic, behind a portico designed by Andrea Sansovino.

entries.name: Basilica e Complesso dei Santi Quattro Coronati
entries.note: A fortified medieval complex rebuilt after the fire of 1084, its entrance dominated by the Torre Maggiore and its Cosmatesque pavement still in place.

entries.name: Aula Gotica dei Santi Quattro Coronati
entries.note: Three hundred square metres of thirteenth-century painting uncovered in 1995, shown on sixteen published days in 2026 with timed entries booked by email.

entries.name: Sepolcro degli Scipioni
entries.note: The tomb of the Cornelii Scipiones on the urban stretch of the via Appia, built in the first decades of the third century BC and entered only by booking on 060608.

entries.name: Basilica di San Giovanni a Porta Latina
entries.note: A basilica behind a cedar-shaded forecourt, open every day from 06.30 to 18.00 by its own account, with a twelfth-century fresco cycle of 46 scenes found in 1940.

entries.name: Osteria il Bocconcino
entries.note: Roman home cooking on Via Ostilia; the dishes it names include zucchine ripiene, tagliolini con ragu d'anatra, polpette ebraiche and tordo matto.

entries.name: Hotel Lancelot
entries.note: A three-star hotel on Via Capo d'Africa, which its own site places in the Celio.
